dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that agentic AI selectively reallocates work and that outcomes depend heavily on user expertise rather than tool access alone. It materially extends that proposition with session-level evidence that domain expertise improves steering and success even as agents reduce the need for coding experience, while appropriately declining to infer realised economic value from proxy outcomes.
qs: Across all of our success measures, the more expertise a person exhibits in a session, the more likely it is that the session succeeds.

As in most of our research, we cannot measure real-world outcomes, like whether code written in a session is actually used or discarded thereafter, or whether it produces an economically valuable artifact.

st.t: Observed use: Capability predictions exceed workplace adoption
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between expanding agentic execution and wholesale job displacement: users retain most planning authority, domain expertise improves outcomes, and broader labour-market implications are explicitly conditional rather than established.
qs: In the typical session, the user makes about 70% of planning decisions while Claude makes about 80% of execution decisions.

If these patterns hold across the economy, it suggests that while agentic coding tools may be absorbing some implementation-heavy work, they are also rewarding those with firm understanding of the problems they solve on the job.

kp.k: Interactive coding study offers cross-domain evidence
kp.d: The June 16, 2026 report by Zoe Hitzig and colleagues at Anthropic examines approximately 400,000 interactive Claude Code sessions from approximately 235,000 people between October 2025 and April 2026 using privacy-preserving analysis. It studies tasks, decision-making, inferred expertise and session outcomes, rather than directly measuring restructuring of legal services. Its sample covers CLI, Claude.ai and desktop usage but excludes third-party IDEs, software development kits and headless usage. Unless otherwise noted, classifiers use Claude Sonnet 4.6.
qs: Here, we introduce a framework for describing interactive AI coding-assistant usage: what kind of work is being done, who is doing it, and whether it succeeds.
All classifiers in this report use Claude Sonnet 4.6 unless otherwise noted.
No researcher reads individual transcripts, occupation labels are never linked to identifiable users, and we only observe aggregates over a minimum number of distinct users.

kp.k: Humans retain planning while agents execute
kp.d: People make about 70% of planning decisions and 20% of execution decisions on average. Typical sessions have about four turns; each prompt triggers around 10 Claude actions on average and 2,400 words of output. Claude takes about eight actions per turn when users control over 80% of execution decisions, versus about 16 when Claude controls over 80% of planning decisions. These are observed collaboration patterns, distinct from benchmark measures of autonomous capability.
qs: On average, people make about 70% of the planning decisions but only 20% of the execution decisions (Figure 2).
In practice, there is a clear division of labor in agentic coding––people decide what to build, and the agent decides how to build it.
In each turn, Claude reads files, edits code, runs commands, and writes on average 2,400 words of output.

kp.k: Task expertise matters more than formal coding identity
kp.d: The report measures apparent task-specific expertise on a five-point novice-to-expert scale, using precision of directions, requests for verification and whether the user corrects Claude or vice versa. Expertise is not equivalent to occupation or general ability: an accountant specifying reconciliation requirements can be rated expert despite never having used Python. This operational definition underpins the report's interpretation that domain understanding enables effective agent direction.
qs: The expertise classifier looks for three signals: how precisely the user frames their directions, what they ask Claude to verify, and whether the user tends to correct Claude or Claude tends to correct the user.
A senior engineer asking their first Rust question is a beginner at Rust.

An accountant who has never used Python, but tells Claude exactly which reconciliation rules a Python script must enforce and catches the edge case it mishandles at month-end close, is an expert at that task.

kp.k: Expert users elicit more work per instruction
kp.d: Typical novice prompts generate about five actions and 600 words, compared with 12 actions and 3,200 words for expert sessions. The difference appears within every work mode and task-value band. Associations remain statistically significant after controlling for work mode, task value, month, occupation and model family: each expertise level is associated with 9% more actions and 13% more output, with standard errors clustered by user. These measures capture activity and output, not independently established economic productivity.
qs: In typical novice sessions, each prompt sets off about five Claude actions and roughly 600 words of output, while expert sessions set off action chains more than twice as long (12 actions) carrying five times the output (3,200 words) (Figure 3).
This gap between novice and expert sessions appears within every kind of work and every band of task value.

kp.k: Usage extends beyond software occupations, including legal work
kp.d: Occupation is inferred in about 70% of sessions using contextual signals, explicitly not treating coding itself as evidence of a software occupation. Computer and Mathematical Occupations is the largest inferred group; management, sales and legal occupations are the fastest-growing non-software groups. A lawyer scripting contract-clause checks illustrates the occupation-classification rule, rather than providing a measured legal-work outcome or evidence of legal-sector displacement.
qs: We were able to infer occupation in about 70% of sessions.
The fastest-growing non-software occupation groups in our sample are management, sales, and legal occupations.
A session in which a lawyer builds a script to automatically flag missing clauses across a folder of contracts is mapped into Legal Occupations, even if the session’s work is primarily software.

kp.k: Work shifts from debugging toward broader agentic tasks
kp.d: Across the sample, writing, fixing, testing and orchestrating code comprise about 56% of sessions, operating software 17%, planning or exploring 14%, and analysis or prose 13%. Between October 2025 and April 2026, fixing broken code falls from 33% to 19%, operating software rises from 14% to 21%, and writing and data analysis roughly double from about 10% to 20%. The report interprets this as movement toward more end-to-end agentic use.
qs: The clearest change is that the share of sessions spent fixing broken code fell from 33% to 19% (Figure 4).
Operating software grew from 14% to 21% of sessions.
Writing and data analysis roughly doubled, from about 10% to 20% of sessions.

kp.k: Estimated task value rises, not demonstrated economic output
kp.d: Using a classifier-based comparison with public freelance job postings, the report estimates that average session task value rose 27% between October and April; its opening summary describes growth as about 25% on average. Estimated building, operating and fixing task values rose about 43%, 34% and 32%, respectively. The authors emphasize relative changes, not literal dollar values, earnings or realized economic benefits; the estimates reflect freelance rather than salaried work and fuzzy matches to job postings.
qs: By this measure, the estimated value of the average session rose by 27% between October and April.
Building, operating, and fixing-type tasks all grew more valuable by roughly a third or more (about 43%, 34%, and 32% respectively).
These price estimates are coarse, so we use them primarily to compare tasks to one another over time, not as dollar values to be read literally.

kp.k: Success measures rely on transcripts, not downstream outcomes
kp.d: Judged success is a classifier's assessment of whether a session achieved its goal. Verified success additionally requires at least one hard success signal, such as relevant git activity or passing tests; companion classifiers assess success and failure evidence. Outcome analyses exclude sessions with no clear goal, about 7.7% of the full sample. This is a study outcome measure, not evidence that a human independently verified all generated work or that the resulting artifact was used successfully.
qs: We do not observe users’ real-world outcomes, and we cannot ask them directly whether they got what they wanted out of Claude.
In particular, it looks for git activity like commits and pull requests matching the work, as well as test suites passing, and explicit affirmation from the user.
For the following analysis, which is focused on the degree of success or failure in a session, we exclude sessions classified as having “no clear goal,” which comprise about 7.7% of our full sample.

kp.k: Competence captures most measured gains from expertise
kp.d: Novice-rated sessions attain verified success 15% of the time and at least partial success 77% of the time; intermediate-or-higher sessions attain verified success 28–33% and partial success 91–92%. Most gains occur between novice and intermediate, with a smaller gap to expert. The analyses compare sessions across work mode, estimated value, month, subject and occupational controls, which the authors describe as partially addressing alternative explanations rather than establishing causation.
qs: Across all of our success measures, the more expertise a person exhibits in a session, the more likely it is that the session succeeds.
A session rated intermediate or up reaches verified success 28-33% of the time and partial success 91-92% of the time (Figure 5).
In each measure, most of the gain comes from moving from novice to intermediate; between intermediate and expert, the slope decreases.

kp.k: Expertise correlates with recovery from agent failures
kp.d: Among sessions encountering trouble, adjusted verified success rises from 4% for novices to 15% for experts; at least partial success is 60% for novices and 80–81% for intermediate through expert users. Troubled sessions are classified as abandoned when judged failed with zero code lines written: 19% for novices versus 5–7% for other levels. The authors qualify these comparisons because experts encounter trouble less often, and their troubled sessions have roughly twice the estimated value of those at the bottom of the expertise scale.
qs: Among sessions that hit trouble, the share that are verified successes rises from 4% for novice-rated sessions to 15% for expert-rated ones, accounting for all the controls described above (Figure 5).
Looking at the looser measures, we find that the share of at least partial success is 60% for novice and 80-81% for intermediate through expert sessions.
Part of the gap in recovery rates may therefore reflect that novices get stuck on routine problems while experts get stuck on challenging hard problems.

kp.k: Occupational success gaps are relatively small
kp.d: Software-related users achieve verified success in about 30% of sessions versus 26% for other professions; in code-producing sessions, rates are 34% versus 29%, with at least partial success at 89% versus 88%. The five-percentage-point verified-success gap stays stable over seven months while both groups improve. Each of the ten largest occupational groups is within seven percentage points of software/math users. Management's slightly higher verified success may reflect transferable delegation skills or a measurement effect from more explicit confirmation.
qs: People in software-related occupations reach verified success in about 30% of their sessions overall, while users from other professions reach verified success about 26% of the time.
That five-point gap is small, and it has neither widened nor narrowed over seven months, even as the success rates in both groups increased.
Their higher verified success rates may reflect management skills that transfer to directing an agent.

kp.k: Labor-market implications remain conditional and preliminary
kp.d: The authors suggest agents may absorb implementation-heavy work while rewarding problem understanding, potentially allowing domain specialists to perform technical work previously beyond their reach. They do not establish employment displacement, wage effects or changes in legal staffing, pricing or professional rules. Their forward-looking framework proposes that declining expertise returns could signal models supplying essential judgment, while growing successful coding outside software occupations could indicate software production becoming ordinary work across fields. Findings remain limited by model-based classifications, incomplete validation, excluded non-interactive activity and unobserved downstream use or economic value.
qs: If these patterns hold across the economy, it suggests that while agentic coding tools may be absorbing some implementation-heavy work, they are also rewarding those with firm understanding of the problems they solve on the job.
These findings are preliminary.

As in most of our research, we cannot measure real-world outcomes, like whether code written in a session is actually used or discarded thereafter, or whether it produces an economically valuable artifact.

For instance, if the returns to expertise begin to decrease over time, that would suggest that models are starting to supply the essential judgment that users currently bring, and that the gains from these tools are broadening beyond domain experts.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Hitzig and co-authors argue that agentic coding delegates implementation to AI while preserving returns to human domain expertise; coding backgrounds appear less important for successful programming.
pts.d: In this cross-domain study, the authors report that users make approximately 70% of planning decisions and 20% of execution decisions. Greater task-specific expertise is associated with more AI activity per instruction, higher session success and better recovery from difficulties. Expert sessions generate about 12 actions and 3,200 words per prompt, compared with five actions and 600 words for novices. Most success gains arise between novice and intermediate expertise, with smaller additional gains from mastery. In code-producing sessions, software-related workers achieve verified success in 34% of sessions versus 29% for other occupations; at least partial success is 89% versus 88%. The authors also report a shift toward operating software, analysis and document production: debugging falls from 33% to 19% of sessions, while estimated average task value rises 27% between October and April, summarized as about 25% in the key findings. They conditionally suggest that agents may absorb implementation-heavy work while rewarding domain understanding. They do not claim demonstrated displacement of lawyers or transformation of legal-service markets.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims draw on Anthropic's observational analysis of approximately 400,000 interactive Claude Code sessions from approximately 235,000 users, using model classifications, telemetry and freelance-market value estimates.
pts.d: Claude-based classifiers infer work mode, decision attribution, task-specific expertise, occupation and success from transcripts. Expertise is inferred from instruction precision, requests for checks and the direction of corrections between user and agent. Occupation is inferred in about 70% of sessions. Judged success is a classifier assessment of whether the user's goal was achieved; verified success additionally requires at least one hard success signal, such as relevant git activity or passing tests. This is a transcript-based outcome measure, not evidence of independent human verification of all output or downstream usefulness. Novice-rated sessions achieve verified success 15% of the time, versus 28–33% for intermediate-or-higher sessions. Among troubled sessions, verified success rises from 4% for novices to 15% for experts. Adjusted comparisons account for observed task and user characteristics. Actions and output remain positively associated with expertise after controls. Task-value estimates use coarse matches to freelance job postings, not observed revenues, wages or realized productivity. The authors report checks against telemetry and reference-model classifications, but acknowledge validation limitations. These are observed associations rather than a causal experiment establishing that expertise causes the differences.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings cover October 2025–April 2026; broader labor-market implications are explicitly preliminary and conditional, without a dated forecast.
pts.d: Published June 16, 2026, the report studies seven months of interactive usage through the CLI, Claude.ai and the desktop app. It excludes third-party IDE, SDK and headless usage, including substantial non-interactive activity. Sessions with no clear goal, about 7.7% of the full sample, are excluded from the success/failure analysis. The authors cannot establish whether session outputs were later used or economically valuable, and all classifications depend on model readings of transcripts. They qualify recovery comparisons because experts encounter trouble less often and their troubled sessions tend to involve harder tasks. They also note that occupational differences may partly reflect communication patterns that make success easier to detect. Generalization to knowledge work depends on the observed patterns holding across the economy. Looking forward, declining returns to expertise would suggest models were supplying more essential judgment; growing successful use outside software occupations could indicate software production becoming part of ordinary work across fields. These are possible future indicators, not established outcomes.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The implicated groups are software professionals, domain experts outside software and novice users; legal occupations appear as a growing user group, not as a separately evaluated legal-services market.
pts.d: Software professionals may face reduced exclusivity over implementation work as workers in other occupations become able to produce code. Domain-competent workers can direct agents to perform technical work without equivalent coding proficiency, while novices obtain less output and are more likely to abandon troubled sessions. Management users have slightly higher verified success than software-related users, which the authors suggest may reflect transferable delegation skills or measurement effects. Management, sales and legal occupations are the fastest-growing non-software groups in the sample. A lawyer writing a contract-clause flagging script is used to illustrate occupation classification, not presented as a documented legal-productivity outcome. The report supplies no separate findings about law-firm staffing, legal fees, clients, access to justice or legal-work quality.
